body:
Why countries need international IP rules

Inventions, goods, services and creative works move across national borders. A company may conduct research in one country, manufacture in another and sell its products in many markets. Different national intellectual property laws can therefore affect international trade, investment and technology transfer.

International agreements create common legal obligations while leaving countries responsible for administering and enforcing many rights through their own systems. They do not normally replace national patent offices or create a single patent valid everywhere.

Meaning and origin of TRIPS

TRIPS stands for the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights. It is a legally binding agreement administered within the framework of the World Trade Organization (WTO).

TRIPS forms Annex 1C to the Marrakesh Agreement Establishing the WTO, signed on 15 April 1994. The WTO began functioning on 1 January 1995, when the WTO agreements, including TRIPS, entered into force.

TRIPS emerged from multilateral trade negotiations and brought intellectual property into the rules-based international trading system. It covers patents, copyright, trademarks, geographical indications, industrial designs, layout-designs of integrated circuits, undisclosed information and the control of certain anti-competitive licensing practices.

Minimum standards do not mean identical laws

TRIPS establishes minimum standards that WTO members must satisfy, subject to its provisions and applicable exceptions or transitional arrangements. Article 1 permits members to provide more extensive protection than the Agreement requires, provided the additional protection does not conflict with TRIPS. Members may choose appropriate methods of implementation within their own legal systems.

Thus, TRIPS does not require every country's patent statute to contain exactly the same words. Nor does it automatically grant a patent merely because a company has obtained a patent in another WTO member.

National treatment and most-favoured-nation treatment

PrincipleTRIPS articleMeaning
National treatmentArticle 3Nationals of other WTO members generally receive treatment no less favourable than a member gives its own nationals concerning IP protection, subject to stated exceptions.
Most-favoured-nation treatmentArticle 4Advantages concerning IP protection given to nationals of one country are generally extended immediately and unconditionally to nationals of other WTO members, subject to stated exceptions.

The 2 principles answer different questions. National treatment compares foreign nationals with domestic nationals. Most-favoured-nation treatment compares the treatment of nationals of different foreign countries.

Patent standards under TRIPS

Article 27 generally requires patents to be available for qualifying inventions, whether products or processes, in all fields of technology, provided the inventions are new, involve an inventive step and are capable of industrial application. The provision contains qualifications and permitted exclusions.

Article 27 also provides that patent rights are to be available and enjoyable without discrimination as to the place of invention, field of technology or whether products are imported or locally produced, subject to the Agreement's provisions. This is a separate legal question from whether the facts of a particular Indian compulsory-licensing application establish insufficient working or supply.

Article 33 requires patent protection to last for a term that does not end before the expiry of 20 years counted from the filing date. The 20-year figure refers to the minimum term required by TRIPS, not a promise that a patent can never lapse earlier for a lawful reason such as non-payment of fees.

Innovation, technology transfer and regulatory space

Article 7 identifies objectives including technological innovation, technology transfer and dissemination, and a balance of rights and obligations. Article 8 recognises that members may adopt measures necessary to protect public health and nutrition and promote public interests in sectors important to socio-economic and technological development, provided such measures are consistent with TRIPS.

Article 40 recognises the possibility of controlling specified anti-competitive practices in contractual licences. The Agreement therefore does not treat all restrictive licensing terms as immune from regulatory examination.

TRIPS also contains development-related provisions. For example, Article 66.2 obliges developed-country WTO members to provide incentives to enterprises and institutions in their territories to promote and encourage technology transfer to least-developed country members. The obligation specifically concerns least-developed countries, not every developing country without distinction.

TRIPS and domestic law

For an Indian inventor, patent rights are obtained and enforced through applicable Indian law. TRIPS creates obligations for India as a WTO member, but the Patents Act, 1970 supplies the domestic procedures for applications, grants, licensing and enforcement.

This distinction explains why an examination question may refer to the same underlying issue at 2 levels: a TRIPS article establishes an international rule, while an Indian statutory section sets out its domestic legal operation.

Prelims focus

  • TRIPS is Annex 1C of the WTO's Marrakesh Agreement, signed on 15 April 1994.
  • The WTO and TRIPS began operating under the WTO framework on 1 January 1995.
  • Article 3 covers national treatment; Article 4 covers most-favoured-nation treatment.
  • Articles 7 and 8 address objectives, public interests and policy principles.
  • Article 33 requires a patent term of at least 20 years from filing.
  • Article 40 concerns anti-competitive licensing practices.
  • Trap: TRIPS minimum standards do not create one worldwide patent.

[Sources: WTO, Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights, preamble and Articles 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 27, 33, 40 and 66.2, amended text as of 23 January 2017, consulted 14 November 2026; WTO, Legal and Interpretive Texts, TRIPS Agreement; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 3, Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal, printed pages 46–47.]

pictures.alt: TRIPS sets international minimum standards; members implement them domestically, with provisions for innovation, public interest and development.
pictures.caption: TRIPS combines common IP standards with qualified national policy choices.

title: The WTO TRIPS Agreement: International Minimum Standards for Intellectual Property

body:
What is a TRIPS flexibility?

A TRIPS flexibility is an option permitted within the TRIPS Agreement that allows a WTO member to pursue a legitimate policy objective while respecting the Agreement's requirements. Such options are especially important for public health, competition and the supply of essential products.

The existence of a patent does not remove every regulatory choice available to a government. At the same time, a government cannot simply disregard all treaty obligations by describing an action as being in the public interest. The relevant legal conditions still matter.

Limited exceptions and compulsory licensing

Article 30 permits certain limited exceptions to the exclusive rights conferred by a patent, provided the exceptions satisfy the conditions laid down in that article. They must not unreasonably conflict with normal exploitation of the patent or unreasonably prejudice the patent owner's legitimate interests, taking account of the legitimate interests of third parties.

Article 31 addresses other use of a patented invention without the authorisation of its right holder, including compulsory licensing and government use. The Agreement permits these measures subject to safeguards.

Important Article 31 safeguards include consideration of authorisation on its individual merits, limits on the scope and duration of permitted use, non-exclusivity and adequate remuneration. Ordinarily, the proposed user must first have tried to obtain authorisation from the right holder on reasonable commercial terms and conditions without success within a reasonable period.

The requirement to seek a voluntary licence first may be waived in specified circumstances, including national emergency, other extreme urgency, public non-commercial use and certain cases involving anti-competitive practices. The patent owner does not thereby lose every legal right.

A national emergency is not a universal precondition for compulsory licensing. Emergency is one circumstance in which special procedural flexibility is available. A member may have other permissible grounds for granting a compulsory licence under its law and the TRIPS framework.

The Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health

On 14 November 2001, WTO members adopted the Doha Declaration on the TRIPS Agreement and Public Health. The declaration affirmed that TRIPS can and should be interpreted and implemented in a manner supportive of members' right to protect public health and promote access to medicines for all.

The declaration clarified important points:

  • Each WTO member has the right to grant compulsory licences and to determine the grounds on which they are granted.
  • Each member may determine what constitutes a national emergency or other circumstances of extreme urgency.
  • Public-health crises, including those involving HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria and other epidemics, may constitute a national emergency or extreme urgency.
  • Members retain policy choices concerning exhaustion of IP rights, subject to the relevant TRIPS provisions on national treatment and most-favoured-nation treatment.

The declaration reaffirmed and clarified existing flexibilities. It should not be described as having created compulsory licensing for the first time.

Exhaustion of rights and parallel imports

Exhaustion concerns the extent to which an IP owner's control over further distribution is affected after a genuine protected product has been placed on the market by the owner or with appropriate authorisation.

Parallel importation generally involves importing genuine goods that have been lawfully marketed elsewhere, without using the brand owner's or patent owner's usual distribution channel in the importing country. It is different from manufacturing counterfeit products.

Article 6 of TRIPS largely leaves members free to establish their own exhaustion regimes, subject to specified obligations, including Articles 3 and 4. Article 3 generally requires treatment of other WTO members' nationals no less favourable than that of domestic nationals; Article 4 generally requires IP advantages granted to one country's nationals to be extended immediately and unconditionally to other WTO members' nationals. Under Indian patent law, Section 107A(b) addresses qualifying imports of patented products from persons duly authorised under the law to produce and sell or distribute them.

Parallel importation and compulsory licensing are separate concepts. Parallel importation deals with the movement of genuine goods already lawfully supplied; compulsory licensing authorises certain patent-protected use without the owner's voluntary permission.

Why pharmaceutical exports needed a special mechanism

Ordinary compulsory licensing under TRIPS Article 31 was generally directed predominantly towards supplying the domestic market. This created a problem for a country that needed affordable medicines but lacked adequate manufacturing capacity: it could not easily benefit from its own compulsory-licensing authority if it could not produce the medicine.

To address this problem, WTO members adopted a 2005 Protocol making permanent the mechanism first established by a 2003 waiver and now found in Article 31bis. The amendment entered into force on 23 January 2017 after acceptance by 2/3 of WTO members. It allows qualifying production and export of pharmaceutical products under special compulsory licences to eligible importing members facing insufficient manufacturing capacity. The amended provisions bind members that have accepted the Protocol; for a member accepting it after its entry into force, they take effect upon that member's acceptance.

India's Section 92A provides a domestic legal route for specified manufacture and export of patented pharmaceutical products where the importing country's public-health and legal conditions are met.

Development and the limits of policy freedom

Public-health measures, competition rules, research exceptions, parallel import policies and technology-transfer incentives demonstrate that international IP law leaves some room for national choices. The permitted scope varies according to the treaty provision and circumstances.

Developing countries may seek to use these options to improve affordability, stimulate local innovation and respond to public needs. Such policies still operate within treaty obligations, domestic laws and the legal requirements applicable to each mechanism.

Prelims focus

  • TRIPS Article 30 concerns limited exceptions to patent rights.
  • Article 31 permits specified use without the patent owner's authorisation, subject to safeguards.
  • The Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health was adopted on 14 November 2001.
  • Article 6 concerns exhaustion of IP rights, which is relevant to parallel imports.
  • The 2005 TRIPS amendment adding Article 31bis entered into force on 23 January 2017.
  • India's Section 92A concerns a special pharmaceutical export mechanism.
  • Trap: Compulsory licensing is not restricted to national emergencies, and the Doha Declaration did not invent it.

[Sources: WTO, TRIPS Agreement, Articles 6, 30, 31 and 31bis and Annex, amended text as of 23 January 2017; WTO, Declaration on the TRIPS Agreement and Public Health, document WT/MIN(01)/DEC/2, paragraphs 4–6, adopted 14 November 2001; WTO, Compulsory Licensing of Pharmaceuticals and TRIPS FAQ, consulted 14 November 2026; Patents Act, 1970, Sections 92A and 107A.]
